name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_STATEMENT_BASED_Q01 - Work done and circular motion in magnetic field

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The magnetic Lorentz force acting on a charged particle moving through a uniform magnetic field does no work on the particle.

Statement II: When a charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field with its initial velocity perpendicular to the field, its trajectory is a circle of constant radius.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Analysis of the First Statement
The magnetic Lorentz force acting on a particle of charge \(q\) moving with instantaneous velocity \(\vec{v}\) in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) is given by \(\vec{F}_m = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\). The instantaneous rate of work done, or power, is \(P = \vec{F}_m \cdot \vec{v} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) \cdot \vec{v}\). Because the vector cross product \(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}\) is strictly perpendicular to \(\vec{v}\), the scalar product is identically zero at every instant (\(P = 0\)). By the work-energy theorem, \(\Delta K = \int P \, dt = 0\), which confirms that the magnetic force performs zero work on the charged particle and its kinetic energy remains constant. Thus, the first statement is scientifically valid.

Step 2: Conceptual Analysis of the Second Statement
When the initial velocity \(\vec{v}\) is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\), the magnetic force has constant magnitude \(F_m = q v B\) and acts perpendicular to the velocity at all times, providing the required centripetal acceleration: \(\frac{m v^2}{r} = q v B\). Solving for the radius of the trajectory gives \(r = \frac{m v}{q B}\). Because the particle's speed \(v\), mass \(m\), charge \(q\), and magnetic field magnitude \(B\) are all constant, the resulting path is a circle of fixed radius. Thus, the second statement is scientifically valid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because both physical assertions are rigorously true, both statements are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_STATEMENT_BASED_Q02 - Interaction between parallel currents and definition of ampere

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Two long straight parallel conductors carrying steady electric currents in the same direction attract each other.

Statement II: The standard SI ampere is defined as that constant current which, maintained in two parallel conductors one metre apart in vacuum, produces a force of \(1 \times 10^{-7}\text{ N m}^{-1}\) on each conductor.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Analysis of the First Statement
Consider two parallel straight conductors carrying currents \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) in the same direction separated by distance \(d\). The magnetic field established by the first wire at the location of the second wire is directed into the plane (by the right-hand rule) with magnitude \(B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}\). Applying the Lorentz force rule \(\vec{F} = I_2 (\vec{L} \times \vec{B}_1)\), the force exerted on the second wire is directed towards the first wire. By Newton's third law, the first wire experiences an equal and opposite force directed towards the second wire. Thus, parallel currents in the same direction attract each other. Hence, the first statement is scientifically valid.

Step 2: Conceptual Analysis of the Second Statement
The magnetic force per unit length between two parallel conductors separated by distance \(d = 1\text{ m}\) carrying equal currents \(I = 1\text{ A}\) in vacuum is given by \(f = \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi d} = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1})(1\text{ A})^2}{2\pi (1\text{ m})} = 2 \times 10^{-7}\text{ N m}^{-1}\). The standard SI definition of the ampere specifies a force of exactly \(2 \times 10^{-7}\text{ N m}^{-1}\), not \(1 \times 10^{-7}\text{ N m}^{-1}\). Hence, the second statement is factually incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because the description of mutual attraction between parallel currents is accurate, whereas the quantitative definition of the ampere gives an incorrect numerical value, the first statement is correct, but the second statement is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_STATEMENT_BASED_Q03 - Solenoid interior field and applicability of Ampere law

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Inside a long, tightly wound current-carrying solenoid, the magnetic field strength increases significantly as one moves from the center towards the open ends along its axis.

Statement II: Ampere's circuital law can be conveniently used to directly evaluate the magnetic field for any arbitrary current geometry without requiring spatial symmetry.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Analysis of the First Statement
Inside an ideal long solenoid carrying current \(I\) with \(n\) turns per unit length, the magnetic field near the central region is uniform and given by \(B = \mu_0 n I\). As one approaches the open ends of the solenoid along its axis, the magnetic field lines flare outward, causing the field strength to decrease, eventually reaching half of the central value (\(B_{\text{end}} \approx \frac{1}{2}\mu_0 n I\)) at the extremities. The field does not increase toward the ends; it decreases. Hence, the first statement is scientifically invalid.

Step 2: Conceptual Analysis of the Second Statement
Although Ampere's circuital law \(\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{\text{enclosed}}\) is mathematically true for any closed path in magnetostatics, it can be applied to directly solve for the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) only in situations possessing a high degree of spatial symmetry (such as infinite straight cylinders, solenoids, or toroids). In systems lacking such symmetry, the field magnitude and orientation vary along the Amperian loop and cannot be factored out of the integral. Thus, the law does not facilitate direct evaluation for arbitrary geometries. Hence, the second statement is scientifically invalid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because the magnetic field inside a solenoid decreases near the ends rather than increasing, and Ampere's law requires high symmetry to evaluate field values, both statements are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_STATEMENT_BASED_Q04 - Cyclotron frequency independence and helical motion kinematics

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The cyclotron frequency of a charged particle revolving in a uniform transverse magnetic field is directly proportional to its kinetic energy.

Statement II: When a charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field at an oblique angle to the field lines, its velocity component parallel to the field remains constant while the perpendicular component undergoes circular motion, resulting in a helical trajectory.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Analysis of the First Statement
For a particle of mass \(m\) and charge \(q\) moving in a uniform magnetic field \(B\), the centripetal condition \(q v B = \frac{m v^2}{r}\) leads to an orbital angular frequency \(\omega = \frac{v}{r} = \frac{q B}{m}\). The cyclotron frequency is \(\nu_c = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{q B}{2\pi m}\). This expression depends solely on the charge, mass, and field strength; it is completely independent of the particle's speed, radius, and kinetic energy (\(K = \frac{1}{2}m v^2\)). Therefore, the claim that the cyclotron frequency is directly proportional to kinetic energy is false. Thus, the first statement is scientifically invalid.

Step 2: Conceptual Analysis of the Second Statement
Resolving the velocity vector into components parallel (\(v_\parallel = v\cos\theta\)) and perpendicular (\(v_\perp = v\sin\theta\)) to the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\), the magnetic force is \(\vec{F}_m = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) = q(\vec{v}_\perp \times \vec{B})\), since \(\vec{v}_\parallel \times \vec{B} = \vec{0}\). Because there is no force along the direction of \(\vec{B}\), the parallel velocity component \(v_\parallel\) remains strictly constant. Meanwhile, \(\vec{v}_\perp\) produces uniform circular motion in the transverse plane with radius \(r = \frac{m v_\perp}{q B}\). The superposition of uniform linear motion along the field and uniform circular motion perpendicular to it produces a helical path of constant pitch. Thus, the second statement is scientifically valid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because the cyclotron frequency is independent of particle energy, while oblique injection indeed produces a helical path with constant parallel velocity, the first statement is incorrect, but the second statement is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: To convert a moving coil galvanometer into an ammeter of a desired higher range, a small resistance known as a shunt is connected in parallel with the coil.

Statement II: Increasing the number of turns of a moving coil galvanometer coil doubles its current sensitivity, but leaves its voltage sensitivity unchanged when using the same wire gauge.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Analysis of the First Statement
A moving coil galvanometer has a relatively high coil resistance \(R_g\) and achieves full-scale deflection with a very small current \(I_g\). To measure a large total current \(I\), a low-resistance path (shunt \(r_s\)) must be placed in parallel with the galvanometer. This parallel arrangement diverts the bulk of the current (\(I - I_g\)) safely away from the sensitive coil and simultaneously minimizes the overall equivalent resistance (\(R_A \approx r_s\)), ensuring that inserting the ammeter into a circuit does not appreciably reduce the current being measured. Thus, the first statement is scientifically valid.

Step 2: Conceptual Analysis of the Second Statement
Current sensitivity is defined as \(I_s = \frac{\phi}{I} = \frac{N A B}{k}\). Doubling the number of turns (\(N \rightarrow 2N\)) doubles \(I_s\). Voltage sensitivity is defined as \(V_s = \frac{\phi}{V} = \frac{N A B}{k R_g}\), where \(R_g\) is the resistance of the galvanometer coil. When the number of turns is doubled using wire of the same gauge, the total wire length doubles, which in turn doubles the coil resistance (\(R_g \rightarrow 2R_g\)). Substituting these into the expression for voltage sensitivity yields \(V_s' = \frac{(2N) A B}{k (2R_g)} = \frac{N A B}{k R_g} = V_s\). Hence, the voltage sensitivity remains unchanged. Thus, the second statement is scientifically valid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because both the shunt requirement for ammeter conversion and the invariance of voltage sensitivity upon doubling the coil turns are established principles, both statements are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_STATEMENT_BASED_Q06 - Net force and torque orientation on planar current loop

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A closed planar current loop placed in any uniform external magnetic field experiences zero net translational force regardless of its orientation.

Statement II: The magnitude of the torque acting on a planar current loop placed in a uniform magnetic field is maximum when the magnetic dipole moment of the loop is parallel to the magnetic field.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Analysis of the First Statement
The net magnetic force on a closed circuit carrying a steady current \(I\) in a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) is given by \(\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = \oint I (d\vec{l} \times \vec{B}) = I \left(\oint d\vec{l}\right) \times \vec{B}\). Because the closed line integral of displacement \(\oint d\vec{l}\) around any closed loop is identically zero, \(\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = \vec{0}\). Therefore, in any uniform magnetic field, the net translational force on the planar loop vanishes regardless of its shape or orientation. Thus, the first statement is scientifically valid.

Step 2: Conceptual Analysis of the Second Statement
The torque exerted on a planar current loop of magnetic dipole moment \(\vec{m} = I\vec{A}\) in a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) is given by the cross product \(\vec{\tau} = \vec{m} \times \vec{B}\), with magnitude \(\tau = m B \sin\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\vec{m}\) and \(\vec{B}\). When \(\vec{m}\) is parallel to \(\vec{B}\) (\(\theta = 0^\circ\)), \(\sin\theta = 0\) and the torque is zero (representing stable equilibrium). The torque attains its maximum magnitude \(\tau_{\text{max}} = m B\) when \(\vec{m}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\) (\(\theta = 90^\circ\)), not when it is parallel. Hence, the second statement is scientifically invalid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because the net force on a closed loop in a uniform field is zero, but the torque is zero (not maximum) when the magnetic moment is parallel to the field, the first statement is correct, but the second statement is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_STATEMENT_BASED_Q07 - Magnetic field profile inside wire and loop axial distance scaling

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Inside a long, straight solid cylindrical conductor of radius \(R\) carrying a uniformly distributed steady current, the magnetic field strength decreases inversely with distance \(r\) from the central axis for \(r \le R\).

Statement II: At a large axial distance \(x\) (\(x \gg R\)) from the center of a flat circular current loop of radius \(R\), the magnetic field strength decreases inversely as the square of the distance \(x\).

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Analysis of the First Statement
For a solid wire of radius \(R\) carrying current \(I\) with uniform current density \(j = \frac{I}{\pi R^2}\), an Amperian loop of radius \(r \le R\) encloses a current \(I_{\text{enclosed}} = j(\pi r^2) = I \frac{r^2}{R^2}\). Applying Ampere's circuital law: \(B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I_{\text{enclosed}} = \mu_0 I \frac{r^2}{R^2} \implies B = \left(\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R^2}\right) r\). This indicates that inside the conductor, the magnetic field strength increases linearly with radial distance \(r\) from the central axis, rather than decreasing inversely with \(r\). Hence, the first statement is scientifically invalid.

Step 2: Conceptual Analysis of the Second Statement
The magnetic field along the axis of a circular loop of radius \(R\) carrying current \(I\) at distance \(x\) from its center is \(B = \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(x^2 + R^2)^{3/2}}\). For points far away along the axis (\(x \gg R\)), this expression reduces to \(B \approx \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2 x^3} = \frac{\mu_0 (2 m)}{4\pi x^3}\), where \(m = I(\pi R^2)\) is the magnetic dipole moment. Therefore, the magnetic field decreases inversely as the cube of the distance (\(B \propto \frac{1}{x^3}\)), not inversely as the square of the distance (\(\frac{1}{x^2}\)). Hence, the second statement is scientifically invalid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because the internal field of the wire increases linearly with radius and the distant axial field of a loop falls off inversely with the cube of the distance, both statements are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOVING_CHARGES_AND_MAGNETISM_STATEMENT_BASED_Q08 - Velocity selector condition and magnetic dipole electrostatic analogy

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A charged particle moving through mutually perpendicular uniform electric and magnetic fields will always pass through undeflected provided its speed is equal to \(E/B\), irrespective of its velocity direction.

Statement II: At large distances compared to loop dimensions, the axial magnetic field of a planar current loop of area \(A\) carrying current \(I\) is mathematically identical to the axial electric field of an electric dipole under the mapping of magnetic moment \(I A\) to electric dipole moment and \(\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\) to \(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\).

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Analysis of the First Statement
Under the Lorentz force law \(\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B})\), a charged particle travels undeflected if and only if the net vector force vanishes: \(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B} = \vec{0}\). This condition requires that the velocity vector \(\vec{v}\) is perpendicular to both \(\vec{E}\) and \(\vec{B}\), and oriented such that the magnetic force \(\vec{F}_m = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\) is directed exactly opposite to the electric force \(\vec{F}_e = q\vec{E}\). If a particle enters with speed \(v = E/B\) in an arbitrary direction (such as parallel to \(\vec{E}\) or parallel to \(\vec{B}\)), the magnetic force does not oppose the electric force and the particle undergoes deflection. Thus, the direction of velocity is critical. Hence, the first statement is scientifically invalid.

Step 2: Conceptual Analysis of the Second Statement
The axial electric field of an electric dipole of moment \(\vec{p}_e\) at large distance \(x\) is \(E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{2 p_e}{x^3}\). For a planar current loop of magnetic dipole moment \(m = I A\), the axial magnetic field at large distance \(x \gg R\) is \(B = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2 m}{x^3}\). Replacing \(\vec{p}_e \rightarrow \vec{m}\) and \(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \rightarrow \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\) directly yields the magnetic field formula from the electrostatic dipole formula, showing exact mathematical correspondence at large distances. Thus, the second statement is scientifically valid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because the velocity selector requires strict directional alignment in addition to the speed condition \(v = E/B\), whereas the dipole correspondence holds accurately at large distances, the first statement is incorrect, but the second statement is correct.

answer.text: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
